summary: An announcement of a one-day workshop at BBN on May 21, 1973 titled Automated Resource Sharing on the ARPANET. The theme was how to move from humans manually using remote resources to processes acting on their behalf, including system-to-system tasks such as file backup.

eli5.summary: A meeting about letting computers, not just people, find and use other computers' services automatically.

subtitle: A workshop to explore how to automate resource sharing across computers on the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: Using remote resources on the ARPANET required manual human intervention; there was no way for programs to find and use resources automatically.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC announces a workshop at BBN in May 1973 to discuss how to move from human-driven resource access to automated process-to-process sharing.
tldr.outcome: The workshop provided a forum to identify obstacles and opportunities for automating resource sharing, including security, accounting, and protocol design.

today: This workshop announcement captured a key moment in networking history: the realization that resource sharing required more than just connectivity. Its emphasis on automation, accounting, and security presaged concerns that remain central to distributed computing and cloud services today.

sections.title: From Manual to Automated Resource Sharing
sections.content: In the early ARPANET era, if a user wanted to use a resource on another system—a compiler, a file system, or a database—they had to manually log in and manage the transfer. The workshop's central question was: how can we move from this human-centric model to one where programs act on behalf of users and systems cooperate with each other?
sections.eli5: People had to manually ask other computers to share their tools and files. The question was how to let computers ask each other automatically.

sections.title: Key Topics for Discussion
sections.content:
The workshop focused on identifying which resources were worth sharing (file systems, compilers, query systems), how to find and select remote resources dynamically, and what obstacles prevented wider sharing.

It also covered practical issues: network-wide accounting so users could use the same account everywhere, security and password management, and the design of protocols that facilitate process-to-process communication rather than just human users.
sections.eli5: The discussions covered what tools could be shared, how to find them, how to bill for them, and how to keep them secure.

sections.title: Approaches to Automation
sections.content: The workshop identified three broad approaches to implementing automated resource sharing. First, multi-site executive programs that make resources accessible at the command level, such as the RSEXEC. Second, programming language environments designed for resource sharing, like a network-aware LISP system. Third, a workshop approach that collects individual tools (an editor here, a file storage service there) and provides unified access.
sections.eli5: There were different ways to do it: special control programs, shared programming languages, or collecting different tools into one place.
